:::{#thm-trace-cyclic}
#### The trace of a product does not depend on the order

For an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ and an $n \times m$ matrix $\matr{B}$:

$$
\tr\paren{\underbrace{\matr{A}\matr{B}}_{m \times m}}
= \tr\paren{\underbrace{\matr{B}\matr{A}}_{n \times n}}
$$

:::

::: proof

$$
\ba
\tr(\matr{A}\matr{B})
&= \sumto{i}{m} (\matr{A}\matr{B})_{ii}
&& \text{(definition of the trace)}
\\
&= \sumto{i}{m} \sumto{s}{n} a_{is}\, b_{si}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \sumto{s}{n} \sumto{i}{m} a_{is}\, b_{si}
&& \text{(swap the order of two finite sums)}
\\
&= \sumto{s}{n} \sumto{i}{m} b_{si}\, a_{is}
&& \text{(multiplication of numbers is commutative)}
\\
&= \sumto{s}{n} (\matr{B}\matr{A})_{ss}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \tr(\matr{B}\matr{A})
&& \text{(definition of the trace)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-trace-cyclic}
#### Traces of the two products of a $2 \times 3$ and a $3 \times 2$ matrix

Let

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The products are

$$
\matr{A}\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{B}\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The trace needs only the diagonal entries.
For $\matr{A}\matr{B}$, which is $2 \times 2$:

$$
\ba
\tr(\matr{A}\matr{B})
&= (\matr{A}\matr{B})_{11} + (\matr{A}\matr{B})_{22}
&& \text{(definition of the trace)}
\\
&= (1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd 2 + 0 \cd 0) + (0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 + 3 \cd 1)
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= (1 + 4 + 0) + (0 + 1 + 3)
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 5 + 4
&& \text{(add within each entry)}
\\
&= 9
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

For $\matr{B}\matr{A}$, which is $3 \times 3$:

$$
\ba
\tr(\matr{B}\matr{A})
&= (\matr{B}\matr{A})_{11} + (\matr{B}\matr{A})_{22} + (\matr{B}\matr{A})_{33}
&& \text{(definition of the trace)}
\\
&= (1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0) + (2 \cd 2 + 1 \cd 1) + (0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 3)
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= (1 + 0) + (4 + 1) + (0 + 3)
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 1 + 5 + 3
&& \text{(add within each entry)}
\\
&= 9
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

The products have different sizes, but their traces agree.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-trace-cyclic-triple}
#### Moving a factor of a triple product

Let $\matr{A}$ be $m \times n$, $\matr{B}$ be $n \times k$,
and $\matr{C}$ be $k \times m$,
so that $\matr{A}\matr{B}$ is $m \times k$
and $\matr{A}\matr{B}\matr{C}$ is square.
Applying @thm-trace-cyclic to the $m \times k$ matrix $\matr{A}\matr{B}$
and the $k \times m$ matrix $\matr{C}$
moves the last factor of the triple product to the front
[@banerjee2014linear, Chapter 1, Theorem 1.5 and eq. 1.17, p. 19]:

$$
\ba
\tr(\matr{A}\matr{B}\matr{C})
&= \tr\paren{(\matr{A}\matr{B})\,\matr{C}}
&& \text{(matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \tr\paren{\matr{C}\,(\matr{A}\matr{B})}
&& \text{(the theorem, applied to the two factors } \matr{A}\matr{B} \text{ and } \matr{C} \text{)}
\\
&= \tr(\matr{C}\matr{A}\matr{B})
&& \text{(matrix multiplication is associative)}
\ea
$$

For example, let

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Then

$$
\matr{A}\matr{B}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd 1 & 1 \cd 0 + 2 \cd 1 \\ 0 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{C}\matr{A}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 0 & 0 \cd 2 + 1 \cd 1 \\ 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 & 1 \cd 2 + 0 \cd 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

so

$$
(\matr{A}\matr{B})\,\matr{C}
= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \cd 0 + 2 \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + 2 \cd 0 \\ 1 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 & 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
(\matr{C}\matr{A})\,\matr{B}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 \\ 1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd 1 & 1 \cd 0 + 2 \cd 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

and both traces are the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tr(\matr{A}\matr{B}\matr{C}) &= 2 + 1 \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tr(\matr{C}\matr{A}\matr{B}) &= 1 + 2 \\
&= 3.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
